newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia-Belarus unity would be costly for Moscow.
newsitem.headline: Russia-Belarus unity would be costly for Moscow.

text.p: A merger of Russia and Belarus could be expensive for Moscow, but economists said on Tuesday that President Boris Yeltsin's offer to consider unity was not an offer of friendship but an order to Minsk to shape up.
Yeltsin sent a letter to Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko on Monday suggesting the two countries hold referendums on a possible merger.
The move is bound to win him political points at home and in neighbouring Belarus, but it is far from clear if a union between the two Slav states could work.
Both were part of the Soviet Union and were founder members of the Commonwealth of Independent States, a loose grouping created when the superpower fell apart.
But the two states have followed different economic paths. Russia is creating a market economy modelled on the West, while Belarussian reforms have barely got off the ground.

"We are diverging more and more from Russia's basic economic principles," Pyotr Lyutko, head of the economic analysis section of Belarus's National Bank, told Reuters. "For instance, we plan to cover our budget deficit in general by printing money."
Printing money to cover the budget deficit is banned in Russia.
Unity could be expensive for Russia -- Belarus is a poor country that has lost Western support.

The International Monetary Fund suspended a stand-by credit to Belarus in January of last year, citing slow reform progress and government control of currency markets and prices. Privatisation has barely started.

Belarus's economy, with about $10 billion gross domestic product for the first 11 months of 1996, is about one thirty-seventh the size of Russia's, official data show. Its $50 monthly average income is about one quarter of Russia's.
"Belarus would be looking for pretty sizeable subsidies from the Russians for a while," said one Western economist.

Gavin Rankin, director of research at Troika-Dialog bank, said Belarus was better off than some of Russia's 89 regions but would offer its bigger cousin few advantages beyond cheaper transit costs for oil and natural gas.
Germany, which absorbed formerly communist East Germany at enormous cost, had a relatively easy unification compared with what Russia and Belarus would face, he said.
"On the one hand you have a major rich country absorbing a weak cousin. Here you have a weak cousin being absorbed by a country that doesn't have the resources to look after itself."

Christopher Granville, United City Bank's head of research, estimated that monetary union with the artificially supported Belarus rouble could cost Russia up to two or three percent of gross domestic product.
But Granville also said Yeltsin may have been sending a political message to Lukashenko in his letter.
"On the political level, Yeltsin has aimed to take away the thunder of his domestic opposition and of Lukashenko himself by running with the referendum idea," he said.
"But...this stage follows a list of things, above all Belarus compliance on customs union."
Russia says Belarus has not upheld its side of a 1995 customs union agreement, a previous step towards unity, which is popular among nationalist Russians and many Belarussians.
Vodka and automobiles imports flow through Belarus into Russia free of customs duties, an enormous loss for Russia.
Elmar Murtazayev, a columnist for liberal daily paper Sevodnya, said Yeltsin's letter was a polite order to Belarus to tighten its borders and consider reform if it wanted unity.
"The proposition looks not so much like help but as a final warning," Murtazayev wrote on Tuesday.
